Five questions to ask before you buy AI listing video

Updated 25 August 2026 · 7 min

AI video from listing photos went from novelty to commodity in about eighteen months. The output ranges from genuinely good to actively damaging, and the difference is not visible in a demo reel — which is the problem, because a demo reel is what you get shown.

These are the five questions that separate the two. Four have a right answer. The fifth is the one worth arguing about.

1. "Does the model see my property, or only my photographs?"

This is the question underneath every quality problem in the category.

Most AI video takes one photo and generates a flight around it. Everything past the edge of that frame is invented: the model is asked what the rest of the building looks like, and it answers confidently. Windows multiply. A second storey appears. The back of the house is a house, just not yours.

The alternative anchors both ends of every shot to real photographs. The model is never asked what the property looks like — it is told, twice, and asked only how a camera gets between the two. It cannot invent the far end of the shot, because the far end is a photograph you supplied.

A good answer sounds like: "every shot starts and ends on one of your images."

A bad answer sounds like: "our model is very accurate."

Accuracy is a claim. Anchoring is a constraint, and constraints are checkable.

2. "Do you edit my photographs?"

It sounds like a question about taste. It is a question about whether your disclosure works.

Under California's §10140.8, a digitally altered image in a property advertisement needs a conspicuous statement and a link to the original, unaltered image. That link points at a page holding your originals.

Now: if your vendor colour-corrects, crops or "enhances" your stills before generating from them, the page they host contains their versions. You are publishing a link that claims to show the unaltered original and does not. The disclosure looks satisfied and isn't.

The right answer is "no, never." Not "only lightly." A vendor who does not touch your files can host them and say truthfully that these are the images you sent.

Worth knowing, because it cuts the other way too: ordinary editing you do yourself is explicitly outside the statute. Lighting, sharpening, white balance, colour correction, angle, straightening, cropping and exposure are all excluded. We wrote that up separately.

3. "What exactly do I get, besides the video?"

The video is the easy part. Ask what arrives with it.

A complete delivery is:

  • the master, and a vertical cut if you post to Reels or TikTok
  • an on-screen disclosure mark
  • a hosted page carrying your unaltered originals, at a real URL
  • a QR code pointing at that page, for print
  • caption text you can paste into the MLS remarks

The third item is the one almost nobody ships, and it is the one the statute actually asks for. A disclaimer in the caption satisfies the first duty and ignores the second entirely.

If the answer is "we give you the file and a suggested disclaimer," you have been sold the easy half and kept all of the liability.

4. "Will you make me a testimonial?"

Say yes to this and you have learned everything you need to know.

The FTC Rule on Consumer Reviews and Testimonials, in force since October 2024, prohibits AI-generated testimonials regardless of disclosure. You cannot label your way out of it. Civil penalties run to tens of thousands of dollars per violation.

A vendor who offers to generate a happy-buyer clip either does not know this or does not care, and both answers tell you how much attention the rest of their compliance thinking has had.

The right answer is a flat no, ideally with the reason attached.

5. "Who owns it, and for how long?"

The one without a single right answer — but there is a right shape.

You want the finished file outright, usable anywhere, indefinitely. Watch for:

  • per-platform licences ("web only", "social only")
  • annual renewals on media you already paid for
  • files that stop working, or get taken down, if you stop subscribing
  • the vendor reusing your property in their own marketing without asking

None of these are automatically unreasonable. All of them should be stated before you buy rather than discovered in a renewal email eleven months later.

The short version

Ask You want to hear
Does the model see the property or the photos? Both ends of every shot are your images
Do you edit my photographs? No, never
What arrives besides the video? A hosted originals page, not just a disclaimer
Will you make me a testimonial? No — and here's the rule
Who owns it? You do, outright, stated up front

None of these are hard questions. That is rather the point: a vendor who has thought about any of this will answer all five in a minute, and one who has not will need to get back to you.

This is not legal advice. The statutory summaries here are drawn from secondary reporting rather than a legal opinion. Read the AB 723 bill text and the FTC's own questions and answers on the Reviews and Testimonials Rule directly, and have your broker's counsel review your disclosure language. Rules vary by MLS and by state.
